cases.abstract: Avoiding quadratic intermediate storage does not remove the normalization and coordination costs of exact attention. FlashAttention-2 reduces these costs by delaying output normalization and exploiting independent query rows. Assigning separate rows to warps avoids forward-pass reductions through shared memory; distributing row blocks across thread blocks exposes parallelism when batches or head counts are small. The implementation retains exact softmax attention with linear additional memory in sequence length. On A100 attention benchmarks covering sequence lengths of 512 to 16k with 16k tokens in total, it runs 1.7-3.0 times faster than FlashAttention. For 1.3B- and 2.7B-parameter GPT-style models trained on eight A100 GPUs at 2k and 8k contexts, whole-model throughput improves by up to 1.3 times over FlashAttention, reaching 225 TFLOPs/s per GPU. Multi-query decoding requires a different response: partitioning key-value cache loads across thread blocks makes its attention kernel up to seven times faster than FasterTransformer. Training gains are larger at 8k than at 2k, showing that kernel acceleration does not translate uniformly into whole-model throughput.
cases.methods: FlashAttention's split-key layout gives each warp only a partial contribution to every output row, requiring shared-memory writes, synchronization, and summation. FlashAttention-2 instead assigns each warp its own query rows while making key and value tiles available to all warps. Since softmax couples scores within a row rather than across rows, each warp can compute complete outputs for its assigned rows without an inter-warp reduction. The same independence permits separate thread blocks to process query-row blocks, increasing occupancy when batches or head counts are small. Within a block, the algorithm tracks a running maximum and exponential sum, rescales an unnormalized output when the maximum changes, and divides only after the last key tile. This avoids repeated denominator scaling while retaining exact softmax attention. Storing rowwise log-sum-exp supports backward recomputation instead of retaining a quadratic probability matrix.
cases.results: The faster attention kernels produce their largest training gains at the longer tested context. On eight A100 80GB GPUs, replacing FlashAttention with FlashAttention-2 raises throughput for a 1.3B-parameter GPT-style model from 189 to 196 TFLOPs/s per GPU at 2k context, but from 170 to 220 at 8k. The 2.7B model reaches 225 at 8k, compared with 175 using FlashAttention. Thus, the strongest training improvement is about 1.3-fold, below the 1.7-3.0-fold attention-kernel gains; accelerating one operation does not imply equal gains for the whole model. Memory feasibility offers a separate comparison: standard PyTorch attention exhausts memory at 16k in the fixed-16k-token benchmark, whereas the tiled implementations complete that setting. The peak reported 72% model FLOPs utilization uses a conventional training formula that does not halve causal attention FLOPs. That percentage describes throughput under the chosen accounting convention rather than directly measuring executed arithmetic.
cases.notes: Abstract connects query-row independence to less communication (Sections 3.2-3.3) and keeps Figure 5's decoding comparison at attention-kernel scope. Methods explains the split-key-to-split-query change and Algorithm 1's delayed normalization; it does not imply synchronization-free backpropagation. Results tests the full-model promise using Table 1's context contrast, retaining Figure 4's PyTorch memory failure and Section 4.3's FLOPs convention. Prospective H100 optimizations and unisolated component-level causal effects remain outside the claims.

cases.abstract: Autoregressive decoding remains serial even when hardware can evaluate several continuations concurrently. Speculative decoding uses a cheap model to propose tokens whose prefixes the target model checks in parallel. Acceptance retains the probability mass shared by the two models; resampling at the first rejection supplies the target mass that remains. This preserves the target sampling distribution for any draft model, without retraining or changing the target architecture. The analysis predicts walltime gains from distributional overlap and proposal cost, assuming independent, identically distributed acceptance rates, sufficiently long generations, and concurrent target evaluations that do not lengthen a target step. In batch-one tests on a single TPU-v4, a 77M-parameter T5-small draft accelerates 11B-parameter T5-XXL over the T5X baseline by 2.6 times for English-German translation and 2.3 times for summarization under standard sampling. Greedy decoding reaches 3.4 and 3.1 times, respectively. Larger tested T5 drafts increase acceptance but yield smaller speedups, revealing a tradeoff between agreement and proposal cost. The latency benefit requires spare parallel compute and can entail more arithmetic work.
cases.methods: Speculative sampling preserves the target distribution without requiring perfect draft agreement. At a fixed prefix, p and q denote target and draft distributions after applying the desired sampling rule. A token x drawn from q is accepted with probability min(1, p(x)/q(x)), contributing mass min(p(x), q(x)). Rejected draws are replaced using the normalized positive part of p - q; weighted by rejection probability, this supplies the remaining target mass. The total is therefore p, regardless of draft quality. The decoder checks prefixes of a gamma-token draft in parallel, retains proposals before the first rejection, and corrects that position. If all pass, it adds a target-sampled token. Each step yields one to gamma + 1 tokens; under independent, identically distributed acceptance rates with mean alpha, the expected yield is (1 - alpha^(gamma + 1))/(1 - alpha), measuring reduced serial target calls rather than reduced computation.
cases.results: Higher acceptance alone does not identify the fastest draft model. For greedy English-German translation at batch size one on a single TPU-v4, T5-small accepts proposals at a rate of 0.75 and speeds up T5-XXL decoding 3.4-fold relative to T5X. T5-large raises acceptance to 0.82 yet achieves only 1.7-fold speedup with the same seven-token draft length. Holding draft length fixed makes the tradeoff clear: the larger model's improved agreement does not offset its proposal cost in this setting. With T5-small, standard sampling lowers translation acceptance to 0.62 and speedup to 2.6-fold; summarization likewise falls from 3.1-fold under greedy decoding to 2.3-fold under standard sampling. The implemented walltime evidence is limited to these T5 tasks; GPT-like and LaMDA evaluations measure acceptance only. Rejected continuations waste target computations, so the latency gains exploit concurrency without establishing a reduction in arithmetic cost.
cases.notes: Abstract separates exact distribution correction from conditional speed predictions (Sections 2.3 and 3.3). Methods makes the accepted-mass/residual-mass argument explicit, then interprets token yield as fewer serial calls, not fewer operations (Sections 3.1 and 3.4). Results uses Table 2's same-seven-token greedy comparison to distinguish acceptance from measured speed and retains the standard-sampling decline. Table 3 supplies only acceptance evidence for GPT-like and LaMDA. Unimplemented adaptive-draft bounds are not presented as measurements.
